assertions: Installing a unit whose name collides with a hand-written skill does not destroy it.
Uninstalling does not delete a hand-written skill through the ledger.
The backfill does not adopt a path it cannot show is a projection.
An ordinary unit still projects, and an ordinary uninstall still removes its own projection.

ticket.found_by: enumerating every writer into a home that does not go through ChildHomeMaterializer
ticket.objective: `<home>/.claude|.codex|.gemini/skills/<name>` is not a skill-manager-only namespace. It is where a human writes skills by hand. Three writers destroyed content there with no warning, no backup, and no mention in any report, and no two of them were in the same file: - the three projectors' apply(), each carrying its own copy of "delete whatever is at the target, then link"; - their remove(), the same six lines inverted; - BindingBackfill, which adopted ANY existing path at a projection target into the projection ledger as though skill-manager had put it there -- after which the ledger-driven LiveInterpreter.reverseProjection deleted it on the next uninstall, believing it was removing its own symlink. The third is the one that makes this a choke-point problem rather than a guard problem: guarding the projectors closed the install door and left the uninstall door open, and the ledger row that authorized the deletion was written by a third file again. Measured that way -- the graph node failed on `uninstall` after the projector fix passed on `install`.
ticket.resolution: ProjectionOwnership, one predicate shared by all three doors: a projection may destroy only a symlink (its bytes live where it points) or a directory the source still holds byte for byte (the copy fallback's own output). Anything else is left alone and named. Deliberately NOT a materialization record. A projection is a pure function of the store, so entitlement is decidable from the two paths alone; a provenance file for it would be machinery nobody needs. Two mechanisms -- ChildHomeMaterializer.Disposal for unit trees, ProjectionOwnership for agent trees -- because the evidence available differs; one rule, because the requirement does not. Projector.apply and .remove became default methods returning whether the write landed, so ProjectorRegistry records only projections that are really there, and a unit whose every projection was held back fails its agent-sync step instead of reporting success.
